final.final_answer:
Verified on MDN via:
- CSS container queries guide
- container-type property reference
- <length> type reference (Container query length units section)

From these pages:

1) Steps required to establish a size-query container
- A size-query container is created by declaring a containment context on the element using container-type with a value that enables size querying:
  - container-type: size;
    - The element becomes a query container whose size-based queries use both its inline and block dimensions.
    - The browser applies layout, style, and size containment to that container.
  - container-type: inline-size;
    - The element becomes a query container whose size-based queries use its inline size only.
    - The browser applies layout, style, and inline-size containment to that element.
  - container-type: normal; (default)
    - Does NOT create a size-query container. The element is not a query container for size queries, though it may still be used for name-only or style queries.
- Once container-type is set to size or inline-size, you then write @container rules that query the container’s size (for example @container (min-width: 700px) { … } or @container (min-inline-size: 40rem) { … }).

2) Difference between size and style queries
From the guide:
- Size queries
  - Apply styles based on the container’s dimensions.
  - Require container-type to be set to size or inline-size so the element is a size query container.
- Style queries
  - Apply styles based on the styles applied to the container (its property values) rather than its physical size.
  - Can use an element as a query container even when container-type remains normal; they do not require size containment.

In short, size queries are driven by measured dimensions of a container that has size containment, while style queries are driven by the container’s styles and don’t require changing container-type away from normal.

3) Container query length units and what each measures
From the “Container query length units” section (CSS container queries guide and <length> reference):
- These units can be used when styling descendants of a container that is a size query container (container-type: size or inline-size).
- They specify a length relative to the dimensions of the query container.

The listed units and meanings are:
- cqw: 1% of a query container’s width.
- cqh: 1% of a query container’s height.
- cqi: 1% of a query container’s inline size.
- cqb: 1% of a query container’s block size.
- cqmin: The smaller of the container’s inline size and block size (1cqmin = 1% of min(inline size, block size)).
- cqmax: The larger of the container’s inline size and block size (1cqmax = 1% of max(inline size, block size)).

4) Fallback behavior and guidance for non-supporting browsers
From the same MDN pages:
- Fallback when no eligible container is available for container query units:
  - “If no eligible container is available for the query, the container query length unit defaults to the small viewport unit for that axis.”
  - That is, cqw/cqi fall back to the corresponding small-viewport width/inline unit; cqh/cqb fall back to the corresponding small-viewport height/block unit; cqmin and cqmax derive from the small-viewport inline and block sizes under the same rule.

- Fallback guidance for browsers that don’t support container queries / container-query units:
  - The “Fallbacks for container queries” section recommends approximating the behavior using:
    - Grid or flex layouts (for example, using grid-template-columns to lay out cards in columns), and
    - Traditional viewport-based media queries to switch layouts at viewport breakpoints (for example, switching from a multi-column card layout to a single-column layout at smaller viewport widths).
  - This combination—grid or flex layout plus media queries—is MDN’s suggested approach when container queries and container query length units are not available.

All four requested points have been verified through visible navigation on the three MDN pages only, without using external search engines.
